verseContext: James writes this to Christians whose arguing and quick tempers were pulling their church family apart.
title: When Anger Knocks
subtitle: You cannot always stop the knocking — but you can choose what you let in
mainTruth: Feeling angry is not a sin, and hiding it does not help. God asks us what we do next — and He helps us, because He is slow to anger Himself.

read.title: Read Together
read.text:
Right near the beginning of the Bible, a man called Cain got angry. His brother had brought God a gift that pleased God, and Cain's had not, and Cain went hot and dark inside. His face fell.

And God came and asked him a kind question — not a telling-off, a question. 'Why are you angry? Why has your face fallen?' Then God said something children remember for the rest of their lives if you say it well: 'Sin is crouching at your door like an animal, waiting to come in. But you can rule over it.'

Cain did not listen. He let it in, and something terrible happened to his brother.

So hold two true things together. First, feeling angry is not the same as doing wrong. Jesus Himself got angry — at people who did not care that a man beside them was suffering, and at traders turning God's house into a marketplace. Jesus was angry and never sinned once. Anger is often a sign that something really is wrong, and God gave us the feeling on purpose.

Second, anger is dangerous the moment it starts giving orders. James, writing to a church full of arguments, put it simply: be quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to get angry.

Notice the order. Listening first. Most children's anger — and most of ours — comes out fast in words before anybody has heard anybody.

So what do you do when anger knocks? You do not pretend you are fine; God is never shocked by a furious child, and pretending only pushes the anger somewhere secret where it grows. You stop. You breathe. You tell God exactly how hot you feel — the psalms are full of people doing precisely that. You tell a grown-up who loves you. And then, when the roaring has gone down, you go and put right whatever needs putting right, today if you can.

And here is the reason any of that is possible. God is 'slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy'. He has had every reason to lose patience with us and He has not. A child who is learning to be slow to anger is not just being well behaved. They are growing to be like their Father.

You cannot always stop anger knocking. You can choose what you let in.
read.childText: Long ago, God asked a man called Cain a kind question. Cain was furious with his brother, and his face went dark and low. God said, 'Why are you angry? Sin is crouching at your door like an animal, waiting to come in — but you can rule over it.' Cain did not listen, and something terrible happened. Now here is something important: feeling angry is not the same as doing wrong. Jesus got angry too, when people were unkind to somebody who was hurting — and Jesus never sinned, not once. Anger is like a knock at the door. You cannot always stop the knocking. But you can choose what you let in. So God says: be quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to get angry. Stop. Breathe. Tell God exactly how hot you feel, because He is never shocked. Tell a grown-up too. And God, who is slow to get angry Himself, will help you.

discuss.title: Talk About It
discuss.question: What can we do when anger comes knocking?
discuss.parentGuide: The new concept is handling anger rightly, and it needs two guard-rails at once. The first misreading is that anger itself is naughty. A child who believes that learns to hide it, feels ashamed of a feeling God gave them, and stops telling you when something is wrong. Jesus was angry and sinless — say that plainly. The second misreading is the opposite: 'I could not help it.' God told Cain he could rule over what was crouching at his door, so the feeling is not in charge. Keep the emphasis on what happens after the knock, not on stopping the knock. Retrieve Two Brothers and Jealous Hearts and let your child notice that God warned Cain kindly first — anger did not surprise God, and neither does theirs. Then admit one time this week when you were slow to listen and quick to speak. Your child already knows about it, and hearing you name it makes the door safe to open.
discuss.familyQuestion: What makes each of us angry fastest, and what helps most?

pray.title: Let's Pray
pray.guidedPrayer: God, sometimes we go hot and cross inside, and You are never shocked by it. Thank You that You are slow to get angry with us. Help us stop, and listen, and put things right. Amen.
pray.childPrompt: Can you tell God exactly what made you angry this week?
prayerPoints: Tell God the honest, hot feeling — He already knows and is not shocked
Ask God to make you quick to listen and slow to get angry

remember.title: Remember This
remember.memoryVerse: Be quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to get angry.
remember.tip: Breathe in slowly while you count to four on your fingers, then let the breath out even more slowly and say: 'Slow to get angry.' Do it three times.

doToday.title: Do It Today
doToday.action: The next time you feel angry today, do one thing before you say anything: take four slow breaths. Then tell somebody how you feel using words, not hands.
doToday.parentNote: Agree a signal together now, before anybody is cross — a hand on the chest, or the word 'four'. Use it on yourself in front of them at least once. And when they manage it, notice the pause out loud rather than the good behaviour that followed.
